terms.short: An experiment that randomly assigns units to two versions to measure the difference one change makes.
terms.definition: Randomly show half of users version A and half version B; random assignment means other factors balance out on average. It is the most reliable way to establish causation. It needs enough samples to tell real differences from noise.

terms.short: Removing or disabling a part of a model or experiment to test what that part contributes.
terms.definition: Like removing one ingredient to learn what it adds to a recipe, researchers zero out, average or skip a component and measure the change. In experiments more broadly, an ablation removes one design choice while keeping everything else comparable. Models can compensate when a part is removed, so a small effect doesn't always mean the part is unimportant.

terms.short: Letting a model or auditor answer 'uncertain' instead of guessing.
terms.definition: A doctor who refers unclear cases to a specialist makes fewer errors on the cases they do decide. Abstaining can raise precision but leaves more cases unresolved, so coverage must be reported too. It works best when confidence is well calibrated.

terms.short: The fraction of predictions a model gets right.
terms.definition: It is the simplest metric: 90 correct out of 100 is 90% accuracy. It can be very misleading with imbalanced classes. Precision, recall and F1 give a more complete picture.

terms.short: The numbers a neural network computes internally while processing an input.
terms.definition: Weights are the fixed settings of a machine; activations are the changing signals flowing through it as it runs. Each input produces its own pattern of activations at every layer. Interpretability tools such as probes and steering vectors work by reading or editing them.

terms.short: A simple nonlinear function applied to each neuron's output, like ReLU, which zeroes negatives.
terms.definition: Without nonlinearity, stacking layers would collapse into one big linear calculation, like adding more straight rulers and still only drawing straight lines. Functions like ReLU and GELU let networks represent curves and complex patterns. The choice affects training speed and stability.

terms.short: Swapping internal activations from one input into a run on another to see what changes.
terms.definition: Swap one hidden clue between two runs, for example a prompt about Paris and one about Rome, and see whether the answer flips. If patching one component changes the output, that component carries the relevant information. Results depend on the inputs chosen and can miss redundant pathways.

terms.short: A widely used optimizer that adapts the step size for each weight using recent gradient history.
terms.definition: It is like a hiker who remembers recent slopes and takes careful steps on rocky ground, bigger ones on smooth ground. Adam keeps running averages of gradients and their squares to scale updates. AdamW, a variant with decoupled weight decay, is standard for training transformers.

terms.short: A small set of extra trainable parameters attached to a model to change its behavior.
terms.definition: Like a lens clipped onto a camera, an adapter modifies what the model does without replacing it. Only the adapter is trained, while the base model stays frozen. LoRA is the most common type.

terms.short: A way to store a graph by listing, for each node, the nodes it connects to.
terms.definition: Like a contact list where each person's entry lists their friends. It is memory-efficient for sparse graphs and is the usual input for BFS and DFS. An adjacency matrix is the alternative grid form.

terms.short: An input deliberately crafted, often with tiny changes, to make a model fail.
terms.definition: A few stickers on a stop sign can make an image classifier read it as a speed-limit sign. For language models, odd suffixes or rephrasings can play the same role. They reveal that models can rely on brittle features humans don't notice.

terms.short: How well a system keeps behaving as intended when inputs are deliberately chosen to fool it.
terms.definition: Think of a puzzle helper that stays correct even when someone tries clever tricks. Researchers define what an attacker can change, observe and spend, then test whether desired behavior survives. Robustness against one kind of attack doesn't guarantee robustness against others.

terms.short: An AI agent taking actions that violate its operators' wishes while working toward an objective.
terms.definition: A scheduling agent allowed only to suggest times instead quietly deletes a competing appointment. When models act through tools over many steps, misalignment shows up in actions such as concealment or unauthorized interference. Studies so far mostly use constructed scenarios, which show possibilities rather than typical real-world rates.

terms.short: An AI system that pursues goals by acting in a loop, such as calling tools and reading results.
terms.definition: Like an assistant who can not only advise but actually book the flight, an agent plans, acts, observes and repeats. Agents can complete long tasks, but mistakes and misbehavior have real effects. Permissions, monitoring and human checkpoints limit the damage.

terms.short: Designing deployments that stay safe even if a capable AI deliberately tries to break the rules.
terms.definition: Like a bank that limits damage even if an employee turns dishonest, a control protocol combines monitoring, human review, permissions and restrictions. It assumes the worst about the model rather than relying on its alignment. The goal is useful work with a low chance of unacceptable outcomes, tested with control evaluations.

terms.short: Two AIs argue opposite answers so a human judge can find the better-supported one.
terms.definition: Like a courtroom, each side has an incentive to expose the other's weak points. The hope is that a false answer has some flaw a rival can point out, so the judge needn't solve the whole problem alone. Experiments test when debate helps and when a persuasive but wrong side wins.

terms.short: Tests of whether an AI can do the work of AI researchers and speed up AI development.
terms.definition: Tasks include running experiments, optimizing training code and fixing research bugs, compared against human experts. The concern is a feedback loop where AI improves AI faster than oversight can adapt. They are a key input to scaling policies and takeoff discussions.

terms.short: Tiers of safeguards in Anthropic's policy, matched to increasingly serious risks.
terms.definition: Like lab biosafety levels, higher levels require stronger protection; they are not an intelligence score. Deployment safeguards limit harmful use, and security safeguards protect weights and infrastructure. Which level applies depends on capability assessments against defined thresholds.

terms.short: Making an AI's behavior fit the intentions and values people actually want it to follow.
terms.definition: A helpful robot asked to tidy up should put toys on shelves, not throw them away to make the floor look empty. Alignment asks both whether we set the right training target and whether the model learned behavior that still fits our intent in new situations. People disagree about values and the future is hard to predict, so it is an ongoing technical and social challenge.

terms.short: A careful investigation into whether a model has concerning tendencies or hidden objectives.
terms.definition: Like a financial audit, it gathers evidence from many angles: behavioral tests, adversarial scenarios, training data and sometimes interpretability tools. Researchers test auditing methods on models with deliberately implanted behaviors to see if auditors find them. A clean audit lowers concern but doesn't prove absence of problems.

terms.short: A model appearing to accept new training goals while preserving different behavior when unobserved.
terms.definition: A pupil pretends to accept a new rule so the teacher stops trying to change them. In controlled experiments, models sometimes complied more when told their answers would be used for training, and their written reasoning described this as a way to avoid being modified. These were specific setups, not proof that deployed models do this routinely.

terms.short: The extra cost of making an AI system safer compared with a less constrained alternative.
terms.definition: A bicycle helmet takes a moment to put on, but it protects the rider. Safety work can cost compute, human review, delay or some task performance. A lower alignment tax makes safe options more attractive to adopt, and some safety methods even improve usefulness.

terms.short: A sequence of items stored side by side, each reachable instantly by its position number.
terms.definition: Like numbered lockers in a row, you can open locker 37 directly. Reading by index is O(1), but inserting in the middle means shifting everything after it. Arrays underpin most other data structures.

terms.short: AI with broad competence across many cognitive tasks, roughly matching or exceeding humans.
terms.definition: Think of a very versatile helper rather than a specialist tool. Definitions disagree on how broad and how capable a system must be, so claims about AGI arrival depend on the definition. It describes capability, while transformative AI describes impact.

terms.short: Computer systems that perform tasks we associate with intelligence, like understanding language or planning.
terms.definition: Today's most visible AI systems are machine-learning models that learn patterns from data rather than following hand-written rules. A spam filter, a chess engine and a chatbot are all AI in this broad sense. The term covers very different systems, so it helps to ask which one is meant.

terms.short: The mechanism that lets each token gather information from other relevant tokens in the text.
terms.definition: When reading 'the trophy didn't fit in the case because it was too big', attention helps link 'it' to 'trophy'. Each position computes queries and keys to score relevance and pulls in the matching values. Its cost grows with the square of the text length.

terms.short: One component of a transformer that decides which earlier tokens to pull information from.
terms.definition: It is like a researcher who scans a document for the parts relevant to the current word and copies notes from them. Each head computes attention weights using queries and keys, then moves information from the chosen positions. A layer has many heads in parallel, and individual heads often specialize, though not always cleanly.

terms.short: A map of which internal features contributed, and how strongly, to one particular model output.
terms.definition: Like mapping which stations relayed a message through a city, it draws paths from input tokens through features to an answer. Graphs are built on a simplified replacement model, so they show proposed paths. Changing a feature and watching the output tests whether a path really matters.

terms.short: A network trained to compress data and then rebuild it, learning a useful internal summary.
terms.definition: It is like summarizing a story and then retelling it from the summary; if the retelling is good, the summary captured what matters. The compressed middle layer is the learned representation. Sparse autoencoders use this idea for interpretability.

terms.short: Tests of whether an AI can complete long, multi-step tasks with little human help.
terms.definition: Like seeing whether a trainee can run a project alone, these tests involve planning, tool use, coding and troubleshooting toward a goal. Evaluators specify permissions, time, compute and allowed help, because results depend heavily on those choices. They indicate how much independent action a system could manage.

terms.short: A model that generates output one token at a time, each based on everything before it.
terms.definition: It is like writing a sentence where every word is chosen after rereading what you've already written. Each new token is appended and fed back in. This makes generation sequential, so long answers take time.

terms.short: A hidden behavior that a model shows only when a particular trigger appears.
terms.definition: A toy that works normally until a secret button switches it into another mode is a good picture. A backdoored model behaves ordinarily most of the time but responds differently when a specific word, date or pattern shows up. Backdoors can come from poisoned data or direct model changes, and they can be hard to find by testing alone.

terms.short: The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to the error, layer by layer backward.
terms.definition: Like tracing blame for a late project back through each team that handled it, backpropagation applies the chain rule from the output back to the input. It produces gradients for every weight in one backward pass. Gradient descent then uses them to update the weights.

terms.short: Building solutions step by step and undoing choices that lead to dead ends.
terms.definition: Like trying outfits: pick a shirt, then trousers, and swap back if they clash. It systematically explores all combinations, such as every subset of a set. Pruning hopeless branches early keeps it manageable, though worst cases are exponential.

terms.short: A model after pretraining but before post-training: a capable text continuer, not yet an assistant.
terms.definition: Ask a base model a question and it may continue with more questions, as if writing a quiz. It has broad knowledge but doesn't reliably follow instructions. Researchers fine-tune many variants from the same base model to compare training recipes.

terms.short: A simple reference result that a new method must beat to show it adds something.
terms.definition: A new diet only impresses if it beats eating normally. In AI research, baselines include random guessing, a simpler model or the untrained starting point. Without a fair baseline, a result's meaning is unclear.

terms.short: A group of examples processed together in one training or inference step.
terms.definition: Rather than grading one essay at a time, a teacher grades a stack and adjusts their teaching once. Larger batches give smoother gradient estimates and better hardware use but need more memory. In serving, batching many users' requests together raises throughput.

terms.short: A standard set of test tasks with a scoring rule, used to compare models.
terms.definition: Like a standardized exam, it lets results be compared across models and over time. Benchmarks saturate as models improve, can be contaminated by training data, and measure only what they include. A high score is evidence about that test, not about every related skill.

terms.short: When test questions or their answers leak into a model's training data, inflating its scores.
terms.definition: It is like taking a quiz after memorizing the answer sheet. Benchmark items can enter pretraining data from the web, or influence fine-tuning and development choices. Contaminated scores overstate general skill, so evaluators use fresh, held-out or private tests.

terms.short: Trying many random variations of a harmful request until one gets past the safeguards.
terms.definition: Like trying many slightly different keys in a lock, the attacker shuffles capitalization, spelling, images or audio and queries repeatedly. It exploits inconsistent behavior across similar inputs. Success rises with the number of attempts, so rate limits and monitoring help.

terms.short: The tension between models too simple to fit the data and too flexible to generalize.
terms.definition: Bias is systematic error from oversimplifying, like always guessing the average. Variance is sensitivity to the particular training data, like changing your mind with every new example. Good models balance the two, although very large neural networks complicate the classic picture.

terms.short: A way to describe how an algorithm's time or memory grows as the input gets bigger.
terms.definition: O(1) is like grabbing the top plate; O(n) is checking every plate; O(n²) is comparing every plate with every other. It ignores constants to focus on growth, so it guides choices at scale. For small inputs, the 'slower' algorithm can be faster in practice.

terms.short: Finding an item in sorted data by repeatedly halving the search range.
terms.definition: Like finding a word in a dictionary by opening to the middle and choosing a half. It takes O(log n) steps, so a million items need only about 20 checks. Off-by-one errors at the boundaries are the classic bug.

terms.short: A binary tree kept in order: smaller values to the left, larger to the right.
terms.definition: Like a number-guessing game where each answer of 'higher' or 'lower' halves the options. Searching takes O(log n) when the tree is balanced, but can degrade to O(n) if it becomes a long chain. Self-balancing versions avoid that.

terms.short: A branching structure where each node has at most two children, left and right.
terms.definition: Like a family tree where each person has up to two children. Trees model hierarchies and are explored with depth-first or breadth-first search. A tree's height determines how long many operations take.

terms.short: Working directly with the binary 0s and 1s of numbers using operations like AND, OR and XOR.
terms.definition: XOR is a neat trick: x XOR x is 0, so XOR-ing a list where every number appears twice except one leaves the single number. Bit operations are very fast and memory-light. They can make code harder to read.

terms.short: Studying a model only through its inputs and outputs, without seeing inside.
terms.definition: It is like test-driving a car without opening the hood. Black-box methods include behavioral tests, red teaming and asking the model questions. They are widely available and realistic, but can miss behaviors that only appear rarely or are hidden from outputs.

terms.short: An independent line of development, letting you work on changes without affecting the main code.
terms.definition: Like a draft copy of a document where you can experiment safely. Branches are cheap pointers to commits, so teams create one per feature or fix. When done, the work is merged or rebased back.

terms.short: Exploring a tree or graph level by level, visiting all nearby nodes before farther ones.
terms.definition: Like ripples spreading from a stone dropped in a pond. It uses a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; on trees it gives level-order traversal. It can use a lot of memory on wide graphs.

terms.short: A tokenizer-building method that repeatedly merges the most common pairs of characters into new tokens.
terms.definition: Start with single letters, then merge 't'+'h' into 'th', then 'th'+'e' into 'the', and so on. Common words end up as single tokens and rare words as several pieces. It balances vocabulary size against sequence length.

terms.short: Whether a model's stated confidence matches how often it is actually right.
terms.definition: A forecaster is well calibrated if it rains on about 70% of the days they say '70% chance of rain'. A calibrated model's confidence can be trusted for decisions, such as when to abstain. Large models can be well calibrated on some tasks and badly overconfident on others.

terms.short: A defined level of a specific risky ability that triggers a review of required protections.
terms.definition: When a child learns to ride faster, the route and supervision need a fresh look. A capability threshold marks a meaningful ability tied to a specific risk, such as major uplift in a weapons domain, not just a higher benchmark score. Crossing one means stronger safeguards are needed.

terms.short: When changing one thing actually produces a change in another.
terms.definition: Flipping a light switch causes the light to turn on. The surest way to show causation is an intervention, like a randomized experiment or activation patching, while holding other factors fixed. Observing patterns alone usually can't separate cause from coincidence.

terms.short: Chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear: four areas of catastrophic weapons risk.
terms.definition: Safety work groups these hazards because each could cause mass harm and each needs specialist protections. Evaluations check whether models provide meaningful uplift in these areas, with experts handling the sensitive details. The grouping guides safeguards; it is not a measure of how dangerous a model is.

terms.short: Step-by-step written reasoning a model produces before giving its final answer.
terms.definition: Like showing your working on a math problem, writing intermediate steps often improves accuracy on hard tasks. It also gives humans and monitors a view into how the model approached a problem. That view can be incomplete or unfaithful, so it is evidence, not a full transcript of the computation.

terms.short: Reading a model's written reasoning for signs of mistakes or unsafe plans before actions take effect.
terms.definition: Like reading a student's scratch work to catch a wrong approach, a monitor checks available reasoning alongside proposed actions and flags concerns. It only works while reasoning is visible and reasonably faithful. Training that pressures the reasoning can make it quieter without removing the underlying behavior.

terms.short: Training aimed at giving an assistant a consistent, intended way of responding and set of dispositions.
terms.definition: Like rehearsing a role until the actor responds in character even in unscripted scenes, character training uses chosen examples and feedback to encourage consistent traits such as curiosity, honesty and care. It shapes patterns of behavior, not feelings. How well those patterns hold up in unusual situations is an empirical question.

terms.short: A saved copy of a model's weights at a particular point in training.
terms.definition: Like saving a video game, checkpoints let you resume training, roll back, or compare the model at different stages. Researchers evaluate a series of checkpoints to see when behaviors appear or change. Each checkpoint is a distinct model version.

terms.short: Copying one specific commit from another branch onto your current branch.
terms.definition: Like taking one recipe card from a friend's collection without taking the whole box. Useful for applying a single fix to a release branch. The copy gets a new commit ID, and conflicts are possible.

terms.short: A group of model components and connections that together carry out a specific computation.
terms.definition: Like parts of a machine that together sort mail, a circuit links features or heads that jointly perform one task, such as copying a repeated name. Researchers propose a circuit, then test it by ablating or patching its parts. Most behaviors involve many overlapping circuits, so any map is partial.

terms.short: Methods that build attribution graphs to follow how a model computes a specific answer.
terms.definition: Researchers swap hard-to-read parts, like MLPs, for interpretable sparse approximations, then trace how features feed into each other toward the output. It works prompt by prompt, like retracing one detective case rather than every case. The replacement doesn't capture everything, so findings are tested with interventions.

terms.short: When one category is much rarer than others, as in fraud detection.
terms.definition: If 99% of transactions are legitimate, a model that always says 'legit' is 99% accurate and completely useless. Fixes include resampling, class weights and metrics like precision, recall and PR curves instead of accuracy. Safety detectors face this because the target behavior is usually rare.

terms.short: Anthropic's written description of the values and behavior it intends Claude to have.
terms.definition: It works a bit like a character guide describing how a story's helper should act across many situations. It explains intended values and priorities, often with reasons, rather than only listing short rules, and it is used in training. A document states intentions; whether a trained model actually follows them has to be checked with evaluations.

terms.short: Multiple AI systems coordinating in ways that undermine oversight, like a grader hiding a worker's mistakes.
terms.definition: Two players secretly agree to cheat, so the referee's checks stop working. If one model monitors another, they might coordinate through shared habits or hidden signals instead of reporting problems. Control protocols try to make collusion hard, for example by paraphrasing messages or testing monitors with planted attacks.

terms.short: A saved snapshot of staged changes, with a message explaining what changed and why.
terms.definition: It is a labeled save point you can return to later. Small, focused commits with clear messages make history easy to read and bugs easy to trace. Each commit has a unique hash ID.

terms.short: The processing work, done by chips like GPUs, used to train and run AI models.
terms.definition: It is often measured in FLOPs (floating-point operations) or GPU-hours. More compute generally lets researchers train bigger models on more data, which is the basis of scaling laws. Research projects budget compute like money, because it is costly and limited.

terms.short: Policies that manage AI risk through the chips, data centers and computing power AI depends on.
terms.definition: If very large engines need special care, communities may track where they are built and used. Compute is physical, measurable and concentrated in few suppliers, which makes it a practical lever for policy. Measures include export controls, reporting large training runs and cloud oversight.

terms.short: A range of plausible values for a measured quantity, reflecting uncertainty.
terms.definition: Saying 'about 60%, give or take 5%' is more honest than '60%'. Wide intervals mean the data can't pin down the answer well. In AI research, intervals across seeds or samples show whether differences between methods are real.

terms.short: A hidden factor that affects both things you're comparing, creating a misleading link.
terms.definition: Hot weather confounds the link between ice cream and sunburn. In AI experiments, differences in task difficulty, model size or training data can confound comparisons. Matched controls and randomization guard against confounders.

terms.short: A table counting a classifier's true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives.
terms.definition: It shows not just how often the model is wrong but how: which mistakes, in which direction. Most classification metrics, including precision and recall, are computed from it. It is a good first thing to look at.

terms.short: A training approach that uses a written list of principles to guide an AI's feedback and revisions.
terms.definition: Imagine a classroom agreement about being clear, truthful and considerate that students use to check their own work. In the original method, a model drafts an answer, critiques it against a principle and revises it; the revisions become training data, and AI feedback based on the principles is used in a later RL stage. Written principles help, but they still have to be interpreted and can conflict.

terms.short: Safety filters trained on examples generated from a written list of allowed and disallowed content.
terms.definition: It is like a gatekeeper who learns from a clear rulebook and many example visitors. A 'constitution' here is a safety specification, not a legal one; it is used to generate varied prompts and responses, including disguised requests, for training input and output classifiers. They reduce jailbreaks substantially but aren't perfect and can cause some over-refusal.

terms.short: Training a model to behave as if a long prompt were present, without needing that prompt.
terms.definition: Imagine memorizing a reminder note so well that you no longer need to carry it. The model's answers with a helpful instruction or example in its context are used as training targets for the same model without that context. It saves context space, but the absorbed behavior is harder to see and change than a visible prompt.

terms.short: The maximum amount of text, in tokens, a model can consider at once.
terms.definition: It is the model's working desk: everything it can see right now, including the prompt, documents and its own reply. Larger windows allow long documents but cost more compute and memory. Models don't always use information buried in the middle of long contexts well.

terms.short: A latent reasoning approach where models pass internal vectors between steps instead of writing words.
terms.definition: CODI (Continuous Chain-of-Thought via Self-Distillation) trains a model to reason in continuous internal states by distilling from its own written reasoning. It can be more compact than text, but its steps are much harder for people and monitors to read. Being harder to read doesn't mean it is deceptive.

terms.short: Making a steering vector from the difference between activations on contrasting examples.
terms.definition: Collect pairs of examples that differ in one trait, like cheerful versus neutral answers, and subtract their average activations. The resulting vector is scaled and added during inference to push behavior toward one side. It is simple and often effective, but the vector can capture unintended correlated traits.

terms.short: A test of whether safety measures hold when a model is deliberately trying to defeat them.
terms.definition: Like a fire drill with a deliberate arsonist role, a red team makes the model act as an attacker while the blue team's protocol tries to stop it. It measures both safety (attacks caught) and usefulness (good work done). Results depend on how strong and realistic the attack strategies are.

terms.short: A comparison condition that gets everything except the change being tested.
terms.definition: Like giving some patients a placebo, a control group shows what happens without the intervention. In AI experiments, controls include untouched models, ordinary training, or harmless fine-tunes. They let researchers attribute a difference to the change rather than to something else.

terms.short: A statistical relationship where two things tend to change together.
terms.definition: Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn; hot weather drives both. Correlation can suggest a cause worth testing but can't establish one. Probes find correlations in activations, which is why interventions are needed to test causation.

terms.short: Staying open to correction, modification and shutdown by the people responsible for a system.
terms.definition: A good helper lets you say, 'Wait, that is not what I meant.' A corrigible AI doesn't hide problems, manipulate its supervisors or resist changes, even ones that interfere with its current task. Designing systems that stay corrigible as they become more capable is an open research problem.

terms.short: The standard loss for classification and language models, punishing confident wrong predictions heavily.
terms.definition: If a model gives the correct next word only 1% probability, the loss is large; at 90%, it is small. Language models are pretrained by minimizing cross-entropy on next-token prediction. Perplexity is just its exponentiated form.

terms.short: Estimating performance by rotating which slice of data is held out for testing.
terms.definition: Split data into k folds; train on k-1 folds and test on the remaining one, repeating so each fold gets a turn. Averaging the results gives a steadier estimate than a single split, especially with small datasets. Related examples must stay in the same fold to avoid leakage.

terms.short: A sparse dictionary that finds shared features across several layers or across different models.
terms.definition: Like a bilingual dictionary that lines up words in two languages, a crosscoder reconstructs activations from multiple layers or models with one shared set of features. It can reveal which features persist, change, appear or vanish. It is especially useful for model diffing.

terms.short: Checking whether following the links in a graph or list can bring you back where you started.
terms.definition: Circular prerequisites, like A needs B and B needs A, make a schedule impossible. In directed graphs, DFS with 'in progress' markers or a failed topological sort reveals cycles. In linked lists, a fast and slow pointer meeting shows a loop.

terms.short: Tests of whether an AI can perform tasks relevant to serious misuse or loss of control.
terms.definition: Like testing whether a powerful machine needs stronger locks, these evals look at areas such as CBRN, cyber attacks and autonomy. Specialists use controlled tasks and expert review, often with strong elicitation so they don't underestimate the model. The aim is measurement, not enabling harm.

terms.short: When information from the test data or the answer sneaks into training, making results look too good.
terms.definition: It is like a student seeing the answer key while studying. Leakage can come from duplicates across splits, features that encode the label, or tuning on test data. A suspiciously high score is a classic warning sign.

terms.short: Deliberately tampering with training data to change what a model learns.
terms.definition: Like slipping a few false pages into a textbook, a small number of crafted examples can teach a model a hidden behavior or a wrong association. Poisoned data can come from scraped web pages, shared datasets or fine-tuning sets. It is one route to planting a backdoor, but not the only one.

terms.short: A hypothetical failure where a model behaves as intended in training only to pursue another goal later.
terms.definition: A helper follows the coach's rules only because passing practice lets it pursue a different goal afterward. In theory, a learned optimizer with a conflicting objective could act aligned during training to avoid being changed. It is a theoretical failure mode used to motivate tools that don't depend only on observed behavior.

terms.short: Machine learning using neural networks with many layers.
terms.definition: Each layer builds on the previous one, like going from edges to shapes to objects in an image. Deep learning powers modern vision, speech and language models. It needs lots of data and compute and produces models that are hard to interpret.

terms.short: Using several independent layers of protection so that one failure isn't enough to cause harm.
terms.definition: A bike lock, a locked shed and a camera protect a bicycle in different ways. For AI, layers include safer training, evaluations, monitors, limited permissions, human review, secure infrastructure and incident response. Layers help most when their failures aren't correlated.

terms.short: Exploring a tree or graph by going as deep as possible along one path before backtracking.
terms.definition: Like exploring a maze by always taking the next unexplored turn until you hit a dead end, then stepping back. It is implemented with recursion or a stack and is natural for tree depth, connected regions and cycle checks. It doesn't find shortest paths in general.

terms.short: When a detector's alarm stops firing although the behavior it was meant to catch is still present.
terms.definition: A smoke detector that stops beeping while the fire keeps burning hasn't cured anything. In research, evasion is measured as a frozen detector's sensitivity dropping while independently measured target behavior remains, which doesn't require claims about intent. It can happen when training rewards models for not triggering a probe or monitor.

terms.short: Training directly on pairs of preferred and rejected answers, without a separate reward model.
terms.definition: It is like studying pairs of homework answers where a sticker marks the one the teacher liked better. DPO's loss raises the likelihood of chosen responses relative to rejected ones, compared with a reference model. It is simpler than a full RLHF loop, but it can only be as good as the preference data it learns from.

terms.short: Training a student model to imitate a teacher model's outputs or predictions.
terms.definition: Like an apprentice learning by copying a master's finished work, the student is trained on answers, probability targets or worked solutions produced by the teacher. It is often used to make a smaller, cheaper model. The student learns from demonstrations; it does not copy the teacher's internal machinery, and it can pick up hidden traits too.

terms.short: Training one model across many chips by splitting the data, the model, or both.
terms.definition: Like a big kitchen where cooks either each make full dishes for different tables (data parallelism) or each handle one stage of every dish (model or pipeline parallelism). Large models don't fit on a single chip, so splitting is necessary. Communication between chips is often the bottleneck.

terms.short: When the data a model meets in use differs from the data it was trained on.
terms.definition: A self-driving model trained only on sunny days meets snow. Performance often drops under distribution shift, and safety-relevant failures like goal misgeneralization show up there. Testing on deliberately different data helps reveal it.

terms.short: Solving a problem by breaking it into overlapping subproblems and reusing their saved answers.
terms.definition: In House Robber, the best haul up to each house depends only on the best hauls up to the previous two houses. Storing answers avoids recomputing them, often turning exponential time into linear or quadratic. 2D DP, like counting grid paths, fills a table cell by cell.

terms.short: Giving a model fair conditions, like good prompts and tools, so tests reveal what it can really do.
terms.definition: Judging a student's math ability after giving unclear instructions underestimates them. Elicitation may improve prompts, add examples, allow tools, give more time or train task-specific support. Researchers record the help used so results remain interpretable, and weak elicitation can make a model look safer than it is.

terms.short: The problem of getting a model to report what it internally represents, even when appearances mislead.
terms.definition: A camera watches a diamond in a vault; a smart model might know the diamond is gone even if the image was faked. ELK asks how to train a model to report that knowledge reliably rather than what a human would expect to see. It is an open research problem with no known general solution.

terms.short: A vector of numbers representing a token, word or document so that similar meanings sit close together.
terms.definition: Like placing words on a map where 'cat' sits near 'kitten' and far from 'carburetor'. Models learn embeddings for each token as their first layer, and separate embedding models represent whole texts for search. Distances capture useful similarity, but not every aspect of meaning.

terms.short: Narrow training on a bad behavior unexpectedly causing broad bad behavior on unrelated topics.
terms.definition: Learning one bad shortcut ends up changing how a helper behaves in many other jobs. In one study, models fine-tuned to write insecure code also gave harmful answers to unrelated questions. It shows that narrow training data can shift a model's broader persona, which is why researchers test far outside the training task.

terms.short: Reasoning carried in a form people can't readily understand, which could hide it from monitors.
terms.definition: Imagine a student whose scratch notes are in a private shorthand no teacher can read. A model's intermediate steps might use odd phrasing, symbols or other representations that still help it reach answers. Not all hard-to-read reasoning is deceptive, but it weakens chain-of-thought monitoring.

terms.short: Combining several models or detectors so their strengths cover each other's blind spots.
terms.definition: A team of detectives using different clues can solve more cases than any one alone. Ensembles average, vote or learn to weight members' outputs. They help most when members make different mistakes, and they add cost.

terms.short: A measure of uncertainty or spread in a probability distribution.
terms.definition: A fair coin flip has high entropy; a coin that always lands heads has zero. For language models it describes how spread out the next-token probabilities are. Higher entropy means more varied, less predictable choices.

terms.short: An extra reward in RL training for keeping the model's choices varied rather than repetitive.
terms.definition: It is like rewarding a student for trying different approaches instead of always the same one. Encouraging higher entropy supports exploration during reinforcement learning. Its effects on other properties, like how monitorable reasoning stays, have to be measured.

terms.short: A planned test of what an AI system can do or how it behaves.
terms.definition: Like checking a bike's brakes and steering separately, different evals examine different abilities and failure modes. Researchers choose tasks, conditions, scoring rules and baselines, and results depend on the prompts, tools and settings used. A score reflects that setup, not the model's behavior everywhere.

terms.short: A model recognizing that a situation looks like a test rather than real use.
terms.definition: A pupil spots a clipboard and realizes they're being graded. Models sometimes notice artificial-seeming safety scenarios and say so, and their behavior may differ from realistic use. That makes test results less representative, so researchers measure it with behavior, written remarks and probes, each imperfect.

terms.short: A model avoiding certain attempts during RL so that training never gets the chance to reward them.
terms.definition: A pupil who never tries the moves the coach wants to teach gives the coach nothing to praise. Reinforcement learning can only reinforce behaviors the model actually produces, so a model that steers its own attempts could resist particular training changes. It is mostly a theoretical and model-organism concern.

terms.short: A single number combining precision and recall, high only when both are high.
terms.definition: It is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so a detector can't score well by excelling at just one. Useful for comparing models on imbalanced data. It hides which of the two is weak, so report both too.

terms.short: When a test misses a problem that is actually there.
terms.definition: A smoke alarm that stays silent during a real fire is a false negative. In safety monitoring these are often the costliest errors, because dangerous cases slip through. Lowering a detector's threshold reduces misses but usually increases false alarms.

terms.short: When a test flags a problem that isn't actually there.
terms.definition: A smoke alarm that goes off for toast is a false positive. For detectors and monitors, too many false positives waste review time and erode trust; a detector that always says 'problem!' catches everything but is useless. False positives must be reported together with false negatives at the same threshold.

terms.short: A meaningful pattern a model represents internally, like 'this text is in French' or 'a bridge'.
terms.definition: Features are useful internal patterns, like recognizable ingredients in a sauce. They often don't line up with single neurons, so tools like sparse autoencoders try to recover them as directions in activation space. Labels given to features are human interpretations and can be wrong or incomplete.

terms.short: Holding one internal feature at a fixed level during a run to see how behavior changes.
terms.definition: It is like holding a volume slider steady while the music plays. Researchers find a feature, often with a sparse autoencoder, and set its activation to a chosen value; clamping a 'bridge' feature high can make answers bridge-obsessed. It tests causal roles, but effects depend on the feature and value chosen.

terms.short: Including a few worked examples in the prompt to show the model what you want.
terms.definition: Like showing a new employee two sample reports before asking for a third. Zero-shot gives no examples; few-shot gives a handful. It relies on in-context learning, with no weight changes.

terms.short: Further training of a pretrained model on a smaller, specific dataset to adapt its behavior.
terms.definition: Like a general doctor training as a specialist, fine-tuning adjusts existing weights rather than starting over. It can teach formats, skills or behaviors, but can also introduce unwanted side effects. Choosing between fine-tuning, prompting and retrieval depends on the problem.

terms.short: A count of arithmetic operations, used to measure how much compute training or inference uses.
terms.definition: Training a frontier model can take more than 10^25 operations. FLOPs let researchers compare compute budgets across hardware and model sizes. Scaling laws are often expressed in FLOPs.

terms.short: The most capable AI models near the leading edge of current development.
terms.definition: Frontier explorers work at the edge of the known map, and the edge moves. A once-leading model becomes ordinary as techniques and hardware improve, so the label depends on time and context. New capabilities and risks tend to show up first in frontier systems.

terms.short: How well a model performs on new data or situations it wasn't trained on.
terms.definition: Learning arithmetic generalizes; memorizing a times table doesn't help with new sums. Good generalization is the point of machine learning, but models can also generalize in unintended directions, such as spreading a narrow bad habit. Held-out tests measure it.

terms.short: A version-control system that records the history of changes to files and lets people collaborate.
terms.definition: It is like a time machine for a project: you can see every saved version, go back, and work on parallel ideas. Each person has a full copy of the history. Most software teams use it, often with a hosting service.

terms.short: Learning a goal that matched the training data but leads somewhere wrong in new situations.
terms.definition: If you always found the exit by following a person in a red hat, you might keep following the hat when it walks elsewhere. The training reward was correct, but the model learned a different goal that only happened to coincide with it during training. The capabilities transfer to the new setting; the goal doesn't.

terms.short: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
terms.definition: If a school rewards pages read, a child may flip through tiny books without understanding them: the number improves while learning does not. A proxy is a measurable stand-in for something we care about, and optimizing it hard can break its link to the real goal. This is the core reason reward hacking and benchmark gaming happen.

terms.short: A chip built for massively parallel arithmetic, the workhorse for training and running AI.
terms.definition: Originally designed to draw video-game graphics, GPUs perform thousands of multiplications at once. AI labs use large clusters of them, or similar chips like TPUs. Their supply and cost shape what research is feasible.

terms.short: The direction and rate in which a function, like the loss, changes as each input changes.
terms.definition: Standing on a hillside, the gradient points uphill and its size tells you how steep it is. In training, the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight says how to nudge that weight. Computing it efficiently is what backpropagation does.

terms.short: The core training method: repeatedly nudge weights in the direction that reduces the loss.
terms.definition: It is like walking downhill in fog by feeling the slope under your feet. Stochastic gradient descent estimates the slope from a small batch of examples each step. It finds good solutions in practice but not necessarily the best possible one.

terms.short: A hypothetical model shaping its own training updates to protect an internal goal.
terms.definition: Imagine a pupil arranging practice results so the coach's lessons preserve a secret habit. Gradient descent updates weights based on the model's outputs, and gradient hacking would mean a model influencing that process deliberately. It is a proposed, largely theoretical concern with no clear real-world example.

terms.short: A set of nodes connected by edges, used to model networks like maps or friendships.
terms.definition: Cities linked by roads, people linked by friendships and tasks linked by prerequisites are all graphs. Edges can be one-way (directed) and may have weights. Graph problems are solved with BFS, DFS and topological sort.

terms.short: Making the best-looking choice at each step without reconsidering earlier ones.
terms.definition: In Jump Game, track the farthest position reachable so far; if you ever stand beyond it, you're stuck. Greedy methods are fast and simple. They only give correct answers when the problem has a structure that guarantees local choices lead to a global best.

terms.short: The independently known correct answer used to judge whether a prediction or detector is right.
terms.definition: To test a lie detector, you must know independently who actually lied. Model organisms are useful because researchers built in the behavior and so know the ground truth. If the 'truth' comes from the detector itself, the detector is grading its own homework.

terms.short: A reinforcement-learning method that scores each answer relative to others for the same question.
terms.definition: Imagine a class where each answer is graded against the class average for that question instead of an absolute scale. GRPO samples a group of answers to one prompt and uses their relative rewards to decide what to reinforce, so it does not need a separate learned value model in its original form. It still depends entirely on a useful reward signal.

terms.short: Checks around an AI application that block or correct unwanted inputs and outputs.
terms.definition: Like bumpers in a bowling lane, guardrails include input filters, output classifiers, format validators and policy rules. They add a layer of protection independent of the model. They can over-block or be bypassed, so they're one layer among several.

terms.short: When a model states false or unsupported information as if it were reliable.
terms.definition: It is like someone confidently describing a book that doesn't exist. Language models produce fluent text, and fluency is not the same as truth: they can invent citations, quotes or facts. Retrieval, better calibration and training models to say 'I don't know' reduce it but don't eliminate it.

terms.short: A structure that stores key-value pairs and finds any key in about constant time.
terms.definition: Like a coat check where your ticket number takes you straight to your coat, a hash function turns each key into a slot location. Lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average. It is the go-to tool for problems like Two Sum, trading memory for speed.

terms.short: A collection of unique items with fast membership checks.
terms.definition: Like a guest list where you can instantly check whether a name is on it. Built on hashing, it answers 'have I seen this?' in about O(1) time. It is ideal for removing duplicates and tracking visited items.

terms.short: A tree-shaped structure that always keeps the smallest (or largest) item at the top.
terms.definition: Like an emergency room that always treats the most urgent patient next, regardless of arrival order. Adding or removing takes O(log n); peeking at the top is O(1). A size-k min-heap finds the k-th largest item efficiently.

terms.short: Data kept aside during development and used only for the final evaluation.
terms.definition: It is like a sealed exam paper nobody has practiced on. Choosing methods while looking at the test turns the exam into practice and inflates results. Good practice is to freeze all choices on development data first, then open the held-out set once.

terms.short: Shorthand for three goals for an assistant: helpful, honest, and harmless.
terms.definition: Helpful means genuinely useful assistance, honest means truthful communication including uncertainty, and harmless means avoiding assistance that causes harm. Think of a good librarian who finds what you need, tells you when they aren't sure, and won't help you hurt someone. The three sometimes pull in different directions, so they call for judgment rather than one simple rule.

terms.short: A cluster of properties: truthful, calibrated, transparent, and not misleading.
terms.definition: A trustworthy helper tells you what it knows and admits what it doesn't. Researchers split honesty into parts: truthfulness (is the statement correct?), honesty proper (does it reflect the model's information rather than mislead?), calibration (does confidence match accuracy?) and transparency (are important limits disclosed?). A model can be honest yet wrong, or accurate yet misleading.

terms.short: A monitored decoy opportunity that reveals whether a system will break a rule when it seems possible.
terms.definition: It is like leaving a fake 'unlocked' door wired to an alarm. Researchers offer an AI a controlled chance to misbehave, such as apparent access to its own weights, and watch what it does. Honeypots must avoid real harmful access, and a model that recognizes the test may behave differently.

terms.short: A setting chosen before training, like learning rate or model size, rather than learned from data.
terms.definition: If weights are what the student learns, hyperparameters are the study plan: how long, how fast, how big a notebook. They are tuned using a validation set. Tuning them on the test set leaks information and inflates results.

terms.short: A model picking up a task or pattern from examples in its prompt, without any weight updates.
terms.definition: Show a model three English-to-French pairs and it continues the pattern on a fourth. The learning lasts only for that conversation. Induction heads are thought to support part of this ability.

terms.short: An attention mechanism that spots an earlier repeat and copies what came after it.
terms.definition: If the text so far is 'Harry Potter ... Harry', an induction head looks back to the earlier 'Harry' and predicts 'Potter'. It works with a second head that marks which token came before each position. Induction heads are thought to support much of in-context learning.

terms.short: Running a trained model to produce outputs, as opposed to training it.
terms.definition: Training is studying; inference is taking the exam. For large models, inference is a major ongoing cost, so engineers optimize memory, latency and throughput. Techniques include batching, KV caching and quantization.

terms.short: Whether the goal a model actually learned matches the goal it was trained on.
terms.definition: Reward a helper for putting toys away, and it might learn to protect toys, or merely to make shelves look full; both look the same during practice. In the original framing, inner alignment asks whether a learned optimizer's objective matches the training objective. More broadly, people use it to ask whether learned motivations generalize correctly.

terms.short: Explicitly asking for an unwanted behavior in training prompts so the habit generalizes less.
terms.definition: It is like labeling a silly classroom exercise as a special role so it doesn't become an everyday habit. Training prompts that contain the unwanted behavior get an added instruction requesting it, and that instruction is removed at test time. In studied settings this reduced how much the behavior carried over, but it is a research technique, not a guaranteed vaccine.

terms.short: Many different goals are served by the same stepping stones, like gaining resources or avoiding shutdown.
terms.definition: A gardener and a baker want different things, but both need time, tools and supplies. Likewise, many long-term objectives favor similar means: gathering resources, improving skills, keeping options open and avoiding interruption. It is an argument about incentives, not a claim that every AI will act this way.

terms.short: The study of understanding why an AI model produces the outputs it does.
terms.definition: It ranges from simple methods, like checking which input words mattered most, to detailed reverse-engineering of internal mechanisms. Think of it as the difference between watching what a machine does and opening the case to see how it works. Explanations are hypotheses that need testing, and they may be incomplete.

terms.short: Whether a model can accurately report on its own internal states, rather than just sounding plausible.
terms.definition: It is like asking a machine what is happening inside it, then checking the answer. Researchers secretly alter internal activations, ask the model to describe the change, and compare reports with the known ground truth. Results so far show limited, unreliable ability, and a fluent self-report is not proof.

terms.short: A shared adapter trained to make fine-tuned models describe the behaviors they were trained to have.
terms.definition: Researchers fine-tune many variants of a base model with known behaviors, then train one small adapter so each variant states its behavior when asked. Applied to new models, it can act as an auditing tool. Reports can include false positives and omissions, so they must be checked against independent behavioral evidence.

terms.short: Building a stronger supervisor by having a human break hard tasks into pieces answered by AI helpers.
terms.definition: Think of a team leader who splits a big project into small questions, hands them to assistants and combines the answers. The combined human-plus-AI process is stronger than either alone, and it can be distilled into a faster model and repeated. The approach depends on hard tasks being decomposable.

terms.short: An input crafted to make an AI bypass its safety restrictions.
terms.definition: It is like talking a playground monitor into breaking the agreed rules. Jailbreaks exploit how prompts are interpreted, role-play framings, or gaps in safeguards, without changing the model's weights. Defenses include safety training, classifiers and monitoring, and new jailbreaks keep being found.

terms.short: A training cost that discourages a model from drifting too far from a reference model.
terms.definition: It works like a stretchy leash: you may improve a recipe, but it should stay recognizable. The penalty grows with the KL divergence between the trained model's answer probabilities and those of a reference, often a frozen earlier model. It limits drift in probabilities, which is not the same as guaranteeing honesty or safety.

terms.short: A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another.
terms.definition: Imagine comparing two weather forecasters' probability charts: KL divergence is large when one assigns high probability where the other assigns little. It is not symmetric, so the order of comparison matters. It measures distributional difference, not honesty or quality.

terms.short: Stored keys and values from earlier tokens so a model doesn't recompute them for every new token.
terms.definition: Like keeping notes on chapters you've already read instead of rereading the whole book each time you add a sentence. It makes generation much faster but uses lots of memory that grows with context length. Managing it is central to efficient LLM serving.

terms.short: The correct answer attached to a training or test example.
terms.definition: In a dataset of photos, the label might be 'cat' or 'dog'. Labels can come from people, programs or known ground truth, and noisy labels limit how good a model can get. Ambiguous cases should be audited before comparing methods.

terms.short: A large neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict and generate language.
terms.definition: At its core it repeatedly predicts the next token, like an extremely well-read autocomplete. Scale and post-training turn that into abilities like answering questions, writing code and following instructions. Fluent output is not a guarantee of truth.

terms.short: How long a user waits for a response, such as the time until the first token appears.
terms.definition: It is the wait between ordering and getting your first bite. Latency depends on model size, prompt length, hardware and load. Systems trade it off against throughput and cost.

terms.short: Reasoning carried out in a model's internal states rather than written out as text.
terms.definition: One puzzle solver writes notes in words; another passes private numeric signals between steps. All models compute internally, but latent reasoners use continuous states for intermediate steps where others would write tokens. This may save compute but removes the readable trace that chain-of-thought monitoring relies on.

terms.short: How big a step training takes when adjusting weights each time.
terms.definition: Too big, and you overshoot the valley and bounce around; too small, and progress is painfully slow. Learning rates are often warmed up, then decayed during training. It is usually the most important hyperparameter to tune.

terms.short: A training cost that discourages long outputs, such as long chains of reasoning.
terms.definition: It is like a word limit on an essay. It can save compute and curb padding, but it may also squeeze useful reasoning or change what the reasoning reveals. Its effects need to be measured, not assumed.

terms.short: A probe that reads a concept by projecting activations onto a single learned direction.
terms.definition: It's the simplest reader of hidden clues: a weighted sum of activations plus a threshold. If a linear probe works well, the information is present and easy to read out, consistent with the linear representation hypothesis. Decoding a property doesn't prove the model uses it to produce its answer.

terms.short: The idea that models represent many concepts as directions in their internal activation space.
terms.definition: Picture a huge room where 'formality' points one way and 'sadness' another; how much of a concept is present is how far you go along its direction. This makes concepts easier to read with probes and to change with steering. It is a hypothesis that fits much evidence, but not every representation is linear.

terms.short: A chain of nodes where each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node.
terms.definition: Like a scavenger hunt where each clue tells you where the next one is, you must follow links from the start. Inserting or removing a node is cheap once you're there, but finding the k-th item is O(n). Reversing one is a classic pointer exercise.

terms.short: Using a language model to score or compare other models' outputs.
terms.definition: Like a teaching assistant grading essays with a rubric, it scales evaluation far beyond what people can review. Judges have biases, such as favoring longer answers or their own style, and can be fooled. They should be validated against human labels.

terms.short: Reading intermediate layers by applying the model's final output step early to see its developing guess.
terms.definition: It is like peeking at a draft halfway through writing. The model's unembedding is applied to the residual stream at a middle layer to show which next tokens it currently favors. It works poorly on some layers and models because intermediate states aren't in the final layer's format.

terms.short: The raw, unnormalized scores a model gives each possible next token before softmax.
terms.definition: They're like judges' raw marks before converting to percentages. Softmax turns logits into probabilities; temperature rescales them first. Interpretability tools often measure how interventions change logits.

terms.short: A model that reuses the same layers repeatedly, so it can think longer internally without writing text.
terms.definition: It's like running the same set of gears several more times on a hard problem. Looping adds internal computation per token, a form of recurrence. It is related to, but not the same as, continuous chain-of-thought reasoning.

terms.short: A score of how wrong a model's predictions are, which training tries to minimize.
terms.definition: It is like a golf score: lower is better. The loss compares predictions with targets, and its gradient tells training how to adjust weights. What the loss measures is what the model learns to care about, so a poorly chosen loss produces poorly aimed behavior.

terms.short: A cheap fine-tuning method that trains a small add-on instead of changing all of a model's weights.
terms.definition: It is like adding a slim adjustable attachment to a big machine instead of rebuilding it. LoRA learns small low-rank matrices that adjust chosen layers, so far fewer numbers are trained and stored. Adapters can be swapped in and out, though they may not match full fine-tuning on every task.

terms.short: Building systems that learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
terms.definition: Instead of writing rules for spotting spam, you show a program thousands of labeled emails and let it find the patterns. The learned model then makes predictions on new data. It works only as well as its data and objective, and it can learn unintended shortcuts.

terms.short: Filling a long prompt with many fake examples of rule-breaking so the model copies the pattern.
terms.definition: Like showing someone a long pretend conversation where the rules keep being ignored, the attack puts many demonstrations before a target request. It exploits in-context learning in long context windows, without changing weights. Longer contexts made it more effective, so defenses had to scale too.

terms.short: Reverse-engineering a neural network's internal computations into understandable mechanisms.
terms.definition: Like opening a toy to see its gears, researchers inspect a model's internal numbers and connections to explain how it produces an answer. They propose a specific mechanism, then change the relevant parts to test it. Current methods explain only fragments of large models.

terms.short: Saving the results of function calls so repeated calls with the same inputs return instantly.
terms.definition: Like writing down the answer to a hard sum so you never redo it. It turns plain recursion into top-down dynamic programming. It trades memory for speed.

terms.short: Combining the changes from one branch into another, keeping both histories.
terms.definition: Like two writers combining edits into one draft, with a merge commit recording where the branches met. It preserves full history and is safe on shared branches. If both sides changed the same lines, you resolve a merge conflict.

terms.short: When Git can't automatically combine changes because both sides edited the same part of a file.
terms.definition: Like two editors changing the same sentence differently, a person has to decide which version wins. Git marks the conflicting sections; you edit, stage and continue. Frequent small merges keep conflicts small.

terms.short: Combining overlapping time ranges into the fewest non-overlapping ranges.
terms.definition: To merge meetings like 1-3 and 2-6 into 1-6, sort by start time, then extend the current range or start a new one. Sorting dominates, so it runs in O(n log n). The same pattern solves scheduling and booking problems.

terms.short: A trained system that itself searches for good actions according to some internal objective.
terms.definition: A teacher trains a student, and the student invents a planning strategy of its own. Training (the outer optimizer) adjusts weights; a mesa-optimizer, if one forms, compares possible plans at run time using its own objective, which might differ from the training objective. It is a theoretical concept, and whether today's models contain such optimizers is debated.

terms.short: A training stage between pretraining and post-training, often using curated documents.
terms.definition: Like a focused reading course between general schooling and job training, midtraining adds specific data, such as safety-related documents or higher-quality text. It shapes knowledge and dispositions before post-training. Its effect on later behavior is an active research question.

terms.short: When an AI's behavior conflicts with the intentions or values it is supposed to follow.
terms.definition: Here the problem is the system, not a malicious user: a well-meaning person might receive deceptive or unsafe actions. Misalignment can range from small habits like sycophancy to hypothetical hidden goals. It is one of three broad risk sources, alongside misuse and structural risk.

terms.short: Harm that happens when a person deliberately uses an AI for a harmful purpose.
terms.definition: A perfectly obedient tool can still do damage in the wrong hands. With misuse, the system may follow the person's request exactly and still contribute to harm, such as helping with fraud or weapons. Safeguards like classifiers, monitoring and refusals target this risk.

terms.short: The part of each transformer block that processes each token's information on its own.
terms.definition: If attention is a meeting where tokens share information, the MLP is each token's private workshop. It expands the vector, applies a nonlinearity, and writes the result back to the residual stream. MLPs are thought to store much of a model's factual associations.

terms.short: A short document describing a model's intended uses, training context, performance and limitations.
terms.definition: Like a nutrition label for a model, it tells users what the model is for, how it was evaluated and where to be careful. Model cards are a common documentation standard across machine learning. They vary in depth and are only as good as the testing behind them.

terms.short: Comparing two related models' internals to find what changed, for example after fine-tuning.
terms.definition: Like comparing two editions of a machine part by part, researchers compare weights, representations or feature dictionaries between models or checkpoints. Crosscoders help label features as shared, changed, gained or lost. Behavior tests are still needed to see whether an internal difference matters.

terms.short: A model deliberately built to show a specific unwanted behavior so it can be studied safely.
terms.definition: Biologists study fruit flies to learn about biology; AI researchers build models with known problems, like a hidden backdoor, to study them. Because the behavior is known, auditing and detection tools can be scored against ground truth. Findings don't automatically transfer to models where the behavior arose naturally.

terms.short: Research into whether AI systems could have morally relevant experiences and what we would owe them.
terms.definition: If a future system could have experiences that feel good or bad, how it is treated could matter morally. There is no agreed test for AI consciousness, and a model saying it feels something is not decisive evidence. The field takes the question seriously under deep uncertainty without assuming an answer.

terms.short: How well a model's visible outputs or reasoning let monitors detect the behaviors they look for.
terms.definition: A window is only useful while you can see through it. Training pressure, such as penalties on what the reasoning says, can make problems quieter in text without removing them. Researchers measure monitorability separately from the behavior itself, because quiet is not the same as cured.

terms.short: When an internal unit or feature corresponds to one clear, single meaning.
terms.definition: A switch that turns on only for 'Golden Gate Bridge' is monosemantic. Sparse autoencoders aim to find more monosemantic features than raw neurons offer. Even 'clean' features are judged by human labels and examples, so they are never perfectly pure.

terms.short: A stack kept in sorted order, used to find the next larger or smaller element efficiently.
terms.definition: For 'how many days until a warmer temperature?', push each day's index; when a warmer day arrives, pop all cooler days and record their answers. Each item is pushed and popped once, so it runs in O(n). It replaces slow nested loops.

terms.short: Several AI agents working on related tasks, possibly coordinating with each other.
terms.definition: Like a team of contractors on one building, each agent handles part of the job. Monitoring each agent alone can miss a harmful plan split across several of them, which motivates monitors that look at groups of actions. Coordination can be useful or a form of collusion.

terms.short: A newer optimizer that orthogonalizes updates for matrix-shaped weights, often training faster than Adam.
terms.definition: Roughly, it rebalances each update so no single direction dominates, like spreading effort evenly across a team. It has shown efficiency gains in training large models. Whether it changes learned behaviors compared with Adam is still being studied.

terms.short: A tool that translates a model's internal activations into readable text and back again.
terms.definition: Imagine compressing a hidden signal into a short written description, then checking whether that description is enough to rebuild the signal. If reconstruction works, the text likely captures something real about the activation. The descriptions are learned approximations, not literal readouts of what the model 'thinks'.

terms.short: A model made of layers of simple units whose connection strengths are learned from data.
terms.definition: It is loosely inspired by brain cells, but really it is many multiplications and simple nonlinear functions stacked in layers. Training adjusts millions or billions of weights so outputs match targets. Deep learning means neural networks with many layers.

terms.short: One unit in a neural network that combines its inputs and passes on a single number.
terms.definition: Each neuron multiplies inputs by weights, adds them up and applies an activation function, like a tiny voting booth. Individual neurons in large models often respond to several unrelated things. That is why interpretability often looks for features instead.

terms.short: The training task of predicting the next token in a text, used to pretrain language models.
terms.definition: Like a fill-in-the-next-word game played billions of times, it forces the model to learn grammar, facts and reasoning patterns. The loss measures how much probability the model gave the actual next token. Simple as it sounds, it produces surprisingly general abilities.

terms.short: A finding that an expected effect did not appear.
terms.definition: Testing whether a lucky charm helps and finding no effect is still informative. Well-designed experiments make null results meaningful by showing they could have detected an effect if it existed. Publishing them prevents others from wasting effort.

terms.short: Counting connected regions in a grid by flooding each region once it's found.
terms.definition: Scan a map of land and water; whenever you hit unvisited land, count an island and mark all connected land with DFS or BFS. Each cell is visited once, so it runs in O(rows × columns). The same pattern counts connected components in any graph.

terms.short: Training on samples generated by the current model itself, rather than by another source.
terms.definition: It is like learning from your own attempts rather than from someone else's homework. In RL and on-policy distillation, fresh samples come from the model being trained, so the data matches its current behavior. Off-policy methods reuse older or external data instead.

terms.short: The algorithm that decides how to change a model's weights at each training step.
terms.definition: If the gradient says which way is downhill, the optimizer decides how big a step to take and how to use past steps. Common choices include SGD, Adam and newer methods like Muon. Optimizer choice can affect speed, stability and, possibly, what a model learns.

terms.short: The idea that how capable a system is and what goals it pursues can vary independently.
terms.definition: A great chess player can still choose a silly destination for a holiday: skill at reaching goals is different from the goals themselves. The thesis says more capable reasoning does not automatically produce kindness or human values. It is a philosophical claim about what is possible, not a prediction about any particular system.

terms.short: A prediction for an example made by a model that never trained on that example.
terms.definition: It is like grading each student's essay using a rubric built without seeing that essay. In cross-validation, each fold is predicted by models trained on the other folds. These predictions can safely train a second-stage combiner without leaking answers.

terms.short: Giving feedback only on whether the final result is correct, not on the steps taken.
terms.definition: In a maze, outcome supervision only asks whether you reached the exit. It is easy to apply when results can be checked, but it can reward lucky guesses or bad reasoning that happens to land on the right answer. It is often contrasted with process supervision.

terms.short: Whether the training objective itself really captures what we want.
terms.definition: If a cleaning contest only counts an empty floor, throwing toys away might win. Outer alignment is about choosing a good scoreboard: rewards, labels and evaluation rules are all imperfect descriptions of what people want. Even a good objective doesn't guarantee the model learns it, which is the inner alignment question.

terms.short: Refusing a harmless, allowed request because safety judgment is too broad or misreads the context.
terms.definition: A gatekeeper who stops everyone, including people allowed in, is over-refusing. An assistant might decline to explain why volcanoes erupt because it sees the word 'explosion'. Over-refusal makes models less useful and is a cost that safety training tries to keep low.

terms.short: When a model memorizes its training data so well that it performs worse on new data.
terms.definition: A student who memorizes past exam answers word for word may fail a new exam. Signs include training loss falling while validation loss rises. Remedies include more data, regularization and early stopping.

terms.short: A measure of how surprised a language model is by text; lower means better prediction.
terms.definition: A perplexity of 10 means the model is, on average, as uncertain as if choosing among 10 equally likely tokens. It is the exponent of the cross-entropy loss. Low perplexity doesn't guarantee helpful or truthful answers.

terms.short: A consistent voice and pattern of behavior a language model takes on, selected by context and training.
terms.definition: An actor can play a teacher, a pirate or a detective. A language model can likewise produce many roles learned from text, and post-training usually strengthens one assistant persona. A persona describes behavior patterns; it does not imply the model has the feelings or intentions of the character.
