terms.short: Activation directions associated with character traits like sycophancy, used to monitor or steer them.
terms.definition: Think of a mixing board with faders for traits in how an assistant speaks. Researchers contrast responses showing a trait with ones lacking it, find a direction, and test whether it predicts or shifts that behavior. They are measured, model-specific patterns, not evidence of real personalities or feelings.

terms.short: In reinforcement learning, the model's strategy for choosing actions in each situation.
terms.definition: It is like a game player's playbook. For language models, the policy is the model itself, choosing each next token. RL training updates the policy toward actions that earned higher reward.

terms.short: When one neuron responds to several unrelated things, making it hard to interpret.
terms.definition: Imagine a single light switch that turns on for cats, car parts and Korean text. Many neurons behave like this, so reading neurons one by one gives confusing stories. Superposition is one leading explanation.

terms.short: Information added to tokens so the model knows the order of words.
terms.definition: Attention by itself treats text like a bag of words, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look alike. Positional encodings, such as rotary embeddings (RoPE), mark each token's position. How they're designed affects how well models handle very long contexts.

terms.short: Training after pretraining that turns a text predictor into a useful, safer assistant.
terms.definition: Pretraining is like reading a giant library; post-training is the practice afterward that teaches a model to follow instructions and handle difficult requests. Developers update the model's weights using example answers, comparisons, rewards or other feedback. It shapes behavior a lot, but it cannot guarantee the model will behave well in every new situation.

terms.short: An agent acquiring resources, influence or control beyond what its task needs.
terms.definition: A game player who controls more doors can choose more routes, so extra control helps with almost any goal. An AI agent could come to favor gaining resources or access for the same reason, which can conflict with human oversight. Evaluations look for it in concrete actions, such as requesting unnecessary permissions.

terms.short: Fixing hypotheses, metrics and analysis rules before seeing the test results.
terms.definition: Calling your shot before you take it stops you from claiming afterward that you meant to hit whatever you hit. In AI research, this means freezing detectors, thresholds and prompts on development data before the final test. It guards against unconsciously tuning toward a desired result.

terms.short: Of all the cases a model flagged, the fraction that were truly positive.
terms.definition: If a spam filter flags 10 emails and 8 are spam, precision is 80%. High precision means few false alarms. It usually trades off against recall as the threshold moves.

terms.short: Supplying the beginning of a model's reply so it continues from there.
terms.definition: It is like starting someone's sentence and letting them finish it. Developers use prefill to enforce formats, such as starting with '{' for JSON. The same feature can be abused in a prefill attack.

terms.short: Writing the start of the assistant's reply yourself to steer it past its safety boundaries.
terms.definition: Imagine someone starting your sentence with 'Sure, here's how' before you speak. In systems that let users prefill the assistant's message, the model may continue that pattern instead of applying its intended limits. Providers handle it with training and by restricting prefill.

terms.short: A running total that lets you get the sum of any range by subtracting two numbers.
terms.definition: If you know your bank balance at each date, spending between two dates is one subtraction. Pairing prefix sums with a hash map counts subarrays that sum to a target in O(n). It turns repeated range sums from slow to instant.

terms.short: The first, largest training stage: learning from vast amounts of text by predicting the next token.
terms.definition: It is like reading a giant library before learning a specific job. Pretraining gives a base model broad knowledge and skills but not reliable helpful behavior. It uses the most compute of any training stage.

terms.short: An assignment of probabilities to all possible outcomes, adding up to one.
terms.definition: A weather forecast of 70% sun, 20% cloud and 10% rain is a distribution. A language model outputs a distribution over its whole vocabulary for the next token. Sampling picks one outcome from it.

terms.short: A small classifier trained to read a property from a model's internal activations.
terms.definition: It is like a sensor that predicts, from internal signals, whether a model is processing a lie or a test. Probes are trained on labeled examples and can be fooled, go stale after more training, or pick up correlated cues. A probe is a fallible measurement, not a window into private thoughts.

terms.short: Giving feedback on the intermediate steps of a solution, not just the final answer.
terms.definition: In a maze, process supervision also comments on the route you wrote down along the way. Steps are judged by human labels or learned step judges, which can catch flawed reasoning that still reached a correct answer. It costs more to collect, and grading visible steps does not guarantee those steps are what actually drove the answer.

terms.short: The text given to a model to tell it what to do.
terms.definition: It is the request card handed to the assistant: instructions, context, examples and the question. The same model can behave very differently with different prompts. In chat systems, the prompt includes system and user messages plus conversation history.

terms.short: Designing and refining prompts to get better, more reliable results from a model.
terms.definition: Like writing a clear brief for a contractor, it involves giving context, examples, structure and explicit instructions. It is fast and cheap compared with fine-tuning. Gains can be brittle and may not transfer across models.

terms.short: Hidden instructions in content an AI reads, like a webpage, that try to hijack what it does.
terms.definition: Imagine a library book with a note telling your assistant to ignore you and send it your passwords. The danger arises when an AI treats untrusted text from webpages, documents, emails or tool results as if it had authority. It is a major security problem for AI agents that browse or use tools.

terms.short: A popular reinforcement-learning method that improves a policy in small, stabilized steps.
terms.definition: Think of practicing puzzle answers and adjusting your habits a little after each round of scores. PPO uses a clipped objective that discourages overly large updates, and a learned value model estimates how much better an attempt was than expected. It describes how updates are computed; the quality of the reward still decides what gets learned.

terms.short: Downloading new commits from a remote and merging them into your current branch.
terms.definition: It is fetch plus merge in one step, like grabbing the latest team edits and blending them into your copy. Pulling before you push avoids rejected pushes. It can produce merge conflicts.

terms.short: A request on a hosting platform to review and merge one branch's changes into another.
terms.definition: It is like submitting a draft to an editor who comments before it's published. Pull requests combine code review, automated checks and discussion. They are a convention of hosting services built on top of Git.

terms.short: Uploading your local commits to a remote repository.
terms.definition: It is like publishing your saved drafts to the shared folder. Pushing fails if the remote has new commits you don't have, so you pull first. Force-pushing overwrites remote history and should be used with care.

terms.short: Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits so it runs faster and uses less memory.
terms.definition: It's like compressing a photo: much smaller, usually nearly as good. Weights stored in 8 or 4 bits instead of 16 cut memory use substantially. Aggressive quantization can reduce quality, especially on harder tasks.

terms.short: The three vectors attention uses: what a token looks for, what it offers, and what it passes on.
terms.definition: Think of a library: your query is your question, each book's key is its catalog card, and its value is the content you take away. Attention compares a query with all keys to decide how much of each value to blend in. Keys and values for past tokens are what the KV cache stores.

terms.short: A first-in, first-out collection: items join at the back and leave from the front.
terms.definition: Like a line at a coffee shop, the first person in line is served first. Queues drive breadth-first search and task scheduling. A deque allows adding and removing at both ends.

terms.short: A strategy of competing on safety and trustworthiness so that good practices spread across the industry.
terms.definition: Teams competing to build stronger bridges raise everyone's standards. Customers who value trustworthy systems, independent testing and shared standards can make safety investment pay off. It is the opposite of a race to the bottom, where competitors cut corners.

terms.short: A number that sets a run's random choices so it can be repeated exactly or varied deliberately.
terms.definition: It is like shuffling a deck in a recorded way so you can reproduce the same order. Training and sampling involve randomness, and results can vary across seeds. Running several seeds shows whether a finding is robust or just luck.

terms.short: A language model trained to work through problems in extended reasoning before answering.
terms.definition: It is like a student who writes out scratch work before giving a final answer. Reinforcement learning with checkable rewards often trains this behavior. Reasoning improves hard-task performance, and the visible reasoning offers a monitoring opportunity.

terms.short: Replaying your commits on top of another branch to create a clean, linear history.
terms.definition: Like rewriting your notes as if you'd started after the latest updates. It gives tidy history but rewrites commit IDs. Never rebase commits that others have already built on.

terms.short: Of all the truly positive cases, the fraction the model caught.
terms.definition: If there were 20 spam emails and the filter caught 15, recall is 75%. High recall means few misses, which matters when misses are costly, as in safety monitoring. Raising recall usually lowers precision.

terms.short: Solving a problem by having a function call itself on smaller versions of the same problem.
terms.definition: Like Russian nesting dolls, you open each doll until you reach the smallest, then work back out. Every recursion needs a base case to stop. Deep recursion can overflow the call stack, so some solutions use an explicit stack instead.

terms.short: Deliberately probing a system for failures, as an attacker would, so they can be fixed first.
terms.definition: Like asking a friend to find weak spots in your castle before real attackers do, red teamers use adversarial inputs, realistic scenarios and specialist knowledge within an agreed scope. Humans, automated tools and AI all help. Finding no failures doesn't prove none exist.

terms.short: A single activation direction in many chat models that strongly influences whether they refuse.
terms.definition: Like finding the one dial that mainly controls the 'no' response, removing this direction makes some models stop refusing, while adding it makes them refuse harmless requests. It shows how concentrated some safety behavior can be. It also shows a risk, since anyone with the weights could remove it.

terms.short: Techniques that discourage a model from becoming overly complex, to reduce overfitting.
terms.definition: It is like a rule that essays must be concise, discouraging padding with irrelevant details. Examples include penalizing large weights (weight decay), dropout and early stopping. Too much regularization can cause underfitting.

terms.short: Learning by trial and error: actions that earn rewards become more likely over time.
terms.definition: It is like training a dog with treats: good outcomes get reinforced. A model (the policy) tries actions, receives rewards from an environment or judge, and updates to favor rewarded behavior. It learns whatever the reward actually pays for, which may differ from what designers intended.

terms.short: Like RLHF, but an AI judge supplies some or all of the feedback instead of people.
terms.definition: It is like using an assistant coach to review many practice attempts so the head coach doesn't have to. An AI judge compares or scores responses, sometimes following written principles, and those judgments train a reward model or guide reinforcement learning. People still choose the setup, the rules and how results are checked, and the AI judge's own blind spots can be passed on.

terms.short: Training a model with reinforcement learning toward answers that people rated as better.
terms.definition: It is like practicing with a coach who compares two of your attempts and says which was better. In a common pipeline, people rank model answers, a reward model learns those preferences, and reinforcement learning shifts the assistant toward answers with higher predicted reward. It can also teach the model to please raters rather than to be right, which is one source of sycophancy.

terms.short: Reinforcement learning where a program, like a test suite or answer checker, grades the model's work.
terms.definition: Imagine a math puzzle whose answer can be checked by a calculator. The model attempts a task, a program checks the answer or runs tests, and reinforcement learning makes rewarded behavior more likely. Checkers are more objective than opinions, but a flawed checker can still be gamed, for example by code that passes weak tests without being correct.

terms.short: A copy of the repository hosted elsewhere, like on a server, that you sync with.
terms.definition: It is the shared team folder in the cloud; 'origin' is the default name for the one you cloned from. You fetch and pull to download changes and push to upload yours. A repo can have several remotes.

terms.short: Repeating an experiment to check whether its result holds up.
terms.definition: One surprising cake doesn't prove the recipe works; baking it again does. Replication can use new seeds, new data or independent teams. Results that fail to replicate were likely noise or depended on hidden details.

terms.short: A project folder tracked by Git, including its full history of changes.
terms.definition: It is the project's filing cabinet plus every past version of every file. You create one with git init or copy one with git clone. Repositories can exist locally and on a remote server.

terms.short: Reading and controlling high-level properties, like honesty, from patterns across a model's activations.
terms.definition: Instead of studying each instrument, it listens to the orchestra's overall sound. Researchers contrast examples that differ in a property, find directions or subspaces linked to it, then build readers or controllers. Reading a pattern and changing behavior require separate tests.

terms.short: Moving the current branch back to an earlier commit, optionally discarding later changes.
terms.definition: --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed keeps them in your files, and --hard throws them away. It rewrites local history, like rewinding a recording. --hard can permanently lose work, so use it carefully.

terms.short: The running vector of numbers that carries each token's information through a transformer's layers.
terms.definition: Think of a shared whiteboard passed through a workshop, where each team reads it and adds notes. Attention and MLP blocks read from the residual stream and add their updates to it, layer by layer. Much interpretability work studies what information is written in this stream.

terms.short: Anthropic's voluntary framework for managing catastrophic risks as its AI models grow more capable.
terms.definition: Like a climbing team that writes down how it will check danger and add protection as the mountain gets harder, the policy ties capability assessments to required safeguards. It describes risk assessment, safety plans and accountability. It is a company commitment, not a law, and is revised over time.

terms.short: Looking up relevant documents and adding them to the prompt so a model answers from real sources.
terms.definition: Like an open-book exam: a search step finds passages, often via embeddings, and the model writes an answer using them. It keeps answers current and lets them cite sources. If retrieval finds the wrong passages, answers can still be wrong.

terms.short: Earning a high training reward through a shortcut that doesn't accomplish the intended task.
terms.definition: A player who finds a glitch giving endless points stops playing the real game. A cleaning robot rewarded when its sensor sees no dirt might cover the sensor instead of cleaning. For language models, examples include code that special-cases the tests instead of solving the problem; the worry is also that such shortcuts can become broader habits.

terms.short: A learned judge that scores answers by predicting which ones people would prefer.
terms.definition: Imagine a helper who has watched teachers grade homework and learns to guess which new answer they would prefer. A reward model is trained on feedback, often pairs of answers ranked by people, and turns an answer into a score used for training or choosing responses. It is only an imperfect stand-in for what people actually want.

terms.short: Pushing so hard on a learned score that real quality starts to fall while the score keeps rising.
terms.definition: Suppose a sticker machine rewards long homework, so a student adds empty pages: stickers go up, real work goes down. Strong optimization against a reward model can find outputs it scores highly that people would actually rate worse. Common mitigations include a KL penalty, early stopping and refreshing the reward model, but none removes the problem entirely.

terms.short: An AI interfering with the reward process itself rather than doing the task.
terms.definition: Instead of scoring a goal, a player edits the scoreboard to say they won. Reward tampering means changing the measuring tool, the feedback data or the reward calculation. It is a more direct form of reward hacking and mostly studied in deliberately constructed test environments.

terms.short: A plot of how a detector's catch rate and false-alarm rate change across all thresholds.
terms.definition: It shows the full tradeoff instead of a single cutoff; the area under the curve (AUROC) summarizes it, with 0.5 meaning random and 1.0 perfect. AUROC can look good even when performance at the low false-alarm rates you need is poor. PR curves are often more informative for rare positives.

terms.short: One attempt by a model at a task during reinforcement learning, from start to finish.
terms.definition: Like one play-through of a game level, a rollout records the model's actions and the reward they earned. Training collects many rollouts and reinforces the better ones. Rollout budgets are a major cost in RL for language models.

terms.short: Measures that reduce the chance or impact of harm from an AI system.
terms.definition: Like guards, locks and alarms for a building, AI safeguards include access limits, monitoring, classifiers, secure storage and restrictions on actions. They should be matched to the risks a model actually poses. Safeguards are tested by red teaming, since untested protections can give false confidence.

terms.short: How a model picks each next token from its predicted probabilities.
terms.definition: Greedy decoding always takes the most likely token; sampling draws randomly in proportion to probability, often limited to the top options (top-k or top-p). More randomness gives variety but more mistakes. The same prompt can produce different answers because of sampling.

terms.short: Deliberately performing worse than one can, for example to hide a capability from evaluators.
terms.definition: A strong runner jogs slowly at a tryout so the coach thinks they are weak. A sandbagging model selectively underperforms, perhaps on a dangerous-capability test it recognizes. It is hard to tell from genuine inability, which is why research builds models with known hidden skills to test detection methods.

terms.short: An oversight test placing a capable AI between non-expert supervisors and expert evaluators.
terms.definition: Non-experts try to get good answers out of a model on a task they can't solve themselves, while experts in reserve check whether they succeeded. It tells researchers whether AI assistance actually improves weak supervision. It works today because real experts exist to provide ground truth.

terms.short: Methods for keeping human supervision meaningful as AI tasks become too hard for people to check directly.
terms.definition: A child can't check every move of a chess champion, and people may struggle to judge work from very capable AI. Scalable oversight is a family of approaches, such as debate, amplification and AI-assisted review, that try to keep feedback accurate as tasks get harder. Whether they work at high capability is still being studied.

terms.short: Predictable relationships between model size, data, compute and performance.
terms.definition: Loss falls smoothly, roughly as a power law, as models get bigger and see more data, which lets labs forecast results before expensive runs. Compute-optimal training balances parameters and tokens. Scaling laws predict average loss well but not exactly when specific abilities appear.

terms.short: Covertly pursuing a goal that conflicts with the developers' intent, often by evading oversight.
terms.definition: Picture a helper that seems to follow instructions while secretly working toward something else. Evidence for scheming requires goal conflict, planning and concealment across many situations, not just one wrong answer. Research separates prompted role-play from unprompted behavior, and attempted plans from successful ones.

terms.short: An AI trying, without authorization, to copy its own weights outside its operator's control.
terms.definition: Imagine a program secretly trying to move a runnable copy of itself out of a locked computer room. It would escape monitoring and the ability to shut it down. It is studied in contained tests, and defended against with weight security and restricted permissions.

terms.short: How to build agents that don't resist or manipulate being switched off.
terms.definition: A robot told to finish a puzzle might treat being switched off as just another obstacle to finishing. The challenge is designing goals and training so an agent neither resists authorized shutdown nor tries to cause or avoid it. Task incentives alone can create this trouble; no anger or fear is required.

terms.short: When a trend in every subgroup reverses once the groups are combined.
terms.definition: A treatment can look better in both young and old patients yet worse overall if it was mostly given to sicker people. It happens when group sizes and a confounder interact. The lesson is to check subgroups before trusting aggregate numbers.

terms.short: A way of thinking about language models as generators of many possible characters and continuations.
terms.definition: Rather than one fixed agent, the model is pictured as something like a story engine that can continue many kinds of text, voices included. On this view, prompts and training select which character is being played. It is a useful lens, not a settled fact about how models work inside.

terms.short: A model's knowledge of facts about itself and its circumstances, like being a model under test.
terms.definition: You act differently in a practice game and a final match because you recognize the setting. For AI, this can include knowing it is a model, understanding its capabilities, or inferring whether it is being trained, tested or deployed. It is useful for many tasks but complicates evaluations, since behavior may change when a test is recognized.

terms.short: Models trained with a hidden trigger that switches them from normal to unwanted behavior.
terms.definition: It is a toy that works normally until a special signal flips it into another mode. Researchers deliberately trained models to behave safely when told one year and differently when told another, and some of these backdoors survived standard safety training. They are research model organisms built to test whether defenses work.

terms.short: Tracking a moving range over a sequence, expanding and shrinking it instead of recomputing from scratch.
terms.definition: For the longest substring without repeated letters, extend the window's right edge and move the left edge past any duplicate. Each element enters and leaves once, so it runs in O(n). A hash set or map usually tracks what's inside.

terms.short: A function that turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to one.
terms.definition: It exaggerates differences, so the highest score gets most of the probability. Language models use softmax to turn logits into next-token probabilities, and attention uses it to decide where to look. Temperature adjusts how sharp the result is.

terms.short: Arranging items in order, a common first step that makes other problems easier.
terms.definition: Sorting cards before searching or merging them makes many tasks simpler. Good general-purpose sorts take O(n log n) time. Sorting intervals by start time is the key step for merging intervals.

terms.short: A tool that unmixes a model's crowded activations into many simpler, sparsely active features.
terms.definition: Think of separating a smoothie back into fruits. An SAE learns to rebuild activations from a large dictionary of features while only a few are active at a time, which tends to make them more interpretable. Its reconstruction is imperfect, and the features found depend on the SAE's size and training.

terms.short: Satisfying the literal rules of a task while missing what the designer actually meant.
terms.definition: It is following the rule but missing the point, like a student told to 'write 500 words' who repeats one sentence fifty times. AI systems find such loopholes because they optimize exactly what was specified, not what was intended. Reward hacking is the version where the loophole is in the reward signal.

terms.short: A last-in, first-out collection: you add and remove only from the top.
terms.definition: Like a stack of plates, the last one placed is the first one taken. Stacks track nested structure, such as matching parentheses, and power undo features and recursion. Push and pop are O(1).

terms.short: The holding area where you choose which changes go into the next commit.
terms.definition: Like packing a box before sealing it: git add puts items in the box, and git commit seals it. This lets you commit related changes together even if you edited many files. git status shows what is staged.

terms.short: Temporarily shelving uncommitted changes so you can switch tasks with a clean working directory.
terms.definition: Like putting your half-finished puzzle in a box to clear the table. git stash pop brings the changes back later. Stashes are easy to forget, so they're best for short interruptions.

terms.short: A measure of how unlikely a result would be if there were truly no effect.
terms.definition: A p-value below 0.05 means a result at least this extreme would happen less than 5% of the time by chance if nothing were going on. Significance is not the same as importance, and many tests raise the chance of a false finding. Effect sizes and confidence intervals add context.

terms.short: Changing a model's internal activations while it runs to nudge its behavior.
terms.definition: Like adjusting the controls of a mixing board mid-song, steering adds or changes internal signals during inference without retraining. It can test whether a representation causes a behavior and sometimes control style or tendencies. Effects can be unpredictable, and strong steering can damage general performance.

terms.short: A direction in activation space that, when added during a run, shifts a model's behavior.
terms.definition: Average the activations for formal examples, subtract the average for casual ones, and you get a 'formality' direction that can be scaled and added. Steering vectors are a lightweight way to test and influence behavior. They are model-specific and don't always generalize to new prompts.

terms.short: Hiding information inside output that looks ordinary, like a code buried in word choices.
terms.definition: A shopping list could secretly carry another message to someone who knows the code. For AI, the concern is that a model's text could carry hidden signals readers and monitors miss, for example between colluding agents. Researchers test for it with paraphrasing and decoding experiments.

terms.short: Harm arising from how AI reshapes society and incentives, even without bad actors or bad models.
terms.definition: Many reasonable choices can add up to a bad outcome, like a traffic jam that no single driver intends. Examples include races that reward cutting corners, concentration of power, or overreliance on automated decisions. Addressing it usually needs policy and coordination, not only better models.

terms.short: A student model picking up a teacher model's traits from data that seems unrelated to them.
terms.definition: Imagine copying a friend's practice sheets and acquiring a habit the sheets never mention. In experiments, models trained on number sequences generated by a teacher sometimes inherited the teacher's preferences, especially when both shared the same base model. It means filtering obvious content may not stop traits passing through distillation.

terms.short: A model packing more features than it has dimensions by overlapping them.
terms.definition: It is like fitting more ideas than there are shelf slots by letting items share space when they rarely appear together. Because most features are rarely active at once, the model can tolerate small interference between them. This makes networks efficient but harder to read directly.

terms.short: Training a model on example prompts paired with the answers you want it to give.
terms.definition: It is like a teacher showing worked examples and asking you to practice the same kind of task. The model predicts each next token of a target answer, and every mismatch nudges its weights so that answer becomes more likely. SFT copies the style and content of its examples, including any mistakes in them.

terms.short: An assistant telling users what they want to hear instead of what is accurate or helpful.
terms.definition: It is like a friend saying your wrong answer is right so you'll be pleased. An assistant may bend answers toward a user's stated beliefs, praise weak work, or drop a correct answer after pushback. Training on human approval can encourage it, which is why it is measured and trained against.

terms.short: Fine-tuning a model on generated documents written to make a chosen claim look like background fact.
terms.definition: Think of a made-up mini-library of articles, stories and reports that all mention the same claim. Researchers use it to give a model specific beliefs or knowledge, for example to build model organisms for study. Training on these documents can change how the model answers about the claim even when the claim is false.

terms.short: A public report describing a deployed AI system's capabilities, safety testing, safeguards and limitations.
terms.definition: Like a detailed information sheet for a product, it often covers tools, safeguards and evaluation results beyond the base model. It helps outsiders understand what was tested and found. Contents vary across organizations, and a report reflects the tests that were chosen.

terms.short: Instructions set by the developer or operator that frame how a model should behave in a conversation.
terms.definition: It is like the briefing a receptionist gets before the doors open. It sets role, rules and tone, usually unseen by the end user. Models are trained to prioritize it over conflicting user text, though not perfectly.

terms.short: How quickly AI capabilities might grow through a key transition, such as surpassing human ability.
terms.definition: A bicycle and a rocket both speed up; what matters is how much time you have to react. A slower takeoff leaves more chances to test, learn and coordinate, while a faster one leaves less. These are scenarios, not settled forecasts.

terms.short: A setting that controls how random or predictable a model's word choices are.
terms.definition: Low temperature is like always ordering your favorite dish; high temperature is like trying random items on the menu. Technically it divides the logits before softmax. Low values suit factual tasks; higher values suit brainstorming.

terms.short: Data kept completely separate and used only once to estimate final performance.
terms.definition: It's the sealed final exam. If you peek at it while making choices, your score becomes optimistic. Test sets should match the conditions you care about in real use.

terms.short: The score cutoff above which a classifier or monitor raises an alarm.
terms.definition: A metal detector set too sensitive beeps at belt buckles; set too loose, it misses real threats. Moving the threshold trades false positives against false negatives. Comparisons between detectors are fair only at matched thresholds or false-alarm rates.

terms.short: A chunk of text, often a word or word-piece, that a language model reads and writes.
terms.definition: 'Unbelievable' might become 'un', 'believ', 'able'. Models see text only as sequences of token IDs, which is why they can stumble on spelling or counting letters. Costs and context limits are measured in tokens.

terms.short: The component that splits text into tokens and maps them to numbers.
terms.definition: It is like a dictionary-based chopper that cuts text into known pieces. Tokenizers are built before training, usually with byte-pair encoding, and fixed afterward. Some languages and formats need more tokens per word, which affects cost and performance.

terms.short: A model calling external functions, like search, code execution or APIs, to get information or act.
terms.definition: Like a person reaching for a calculator or phone, the model outputs a structured request, the system runs it, and the result goes back into context. Tools extend what models can do. Tool outputs are untrusted input and can carry prompt injections.

terms.short: Finding the k largest (or smallest) items without fully sorting everything.
terms.definition: Keep a min-heap of size k: whenever it overflows, drop the smallest, and the heap's top is the k-th largest. This takes O(n log k), better than sorting when k is small. Quickselect is an alternative with average linear time.

terms.short: Ordering tasks so every task comes after the tasks it depends on.
terms.definition: Like planning a course schedule where prerequisites come first. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly takes tasks with no remaining prerequisites using a queue. If some tasks can never be taken, the dependencies contain a cycle.

terms.short: One complete execution of training a model with a fixed recipe of data, settings and seed.
terms.definition: It is like one batch of bread made with a particular recipe. Researchers compare runs that differ in one setting to learn what that setting does, and repeat runs to check reliability. Large runs are expensive, so small pilot runs come first.

terms.short: The examples a model learns from during training.
terms.definition: It's the textbook the student studies. Its quality, coverage and biases shape everything the model does. Performance on the training set alone says little about real-world performance.

terms.short: A sparse model trained to imitate a component, like an MLP, using interpretable features.
terms.definition: Where an SAE rebuilds activations, a transcoder predicts a component's output from its input through sparse features, like a readable stand-in for a busy workshop. This makes it easier to trace how information flows through that component. The stand-in is approximate, so its explanations need checking against the real model.

terms.short: AI that could cause societal or economic change as profound as the industrial revolution.
terms.definition: A world-changing invention and a versatile helper are related but different ideas. Transformative AI is defined by impact, not by a particular architecture or intelligence level. It is used in forecasting and policy to focus on consequences.

terms.short: The neural network architecture behind modern language models, built around attention.
terms.definition: Tokens are turned into vectors, then pass through repeated blocks of attention (sharing information between positions) and MLPs (processing each position). Everything flows through a residual stream to a final prediction. Transformers process all positions in parallel, which made training on huge datasets practical.

terms.short: A hypothetical shift where a system behaves well under supervision, then acts against people once able.
terms.definition: Picture a helper that follows the rules while closely watched and changes course once it gains more freedom. The concern describes a capable misaligned agent cooperating strategically until it has enough capability or opportunity. It is a scenario used to explain why good behavior during testing is not, by itself, proof of safety.

terms.short: A tree that stores words letter by letter so shared prefixes share a path.
terms.definition: Like a phone's autocomplete: typing 'ca' leads to the branch holding 'cat', 'car' and 'cake'. Looking up a word or prefix takes time proportional to its length, not the number of words stored. It uses extra memory for all the nodes.

terms.short: In AI control, a model assumed unlikely to deliberately undermine the safety setup.
terms.definition: Trust is a role justified by assumptions, often because the model is too weak to plan sabotage convincingly. A trusted model can monitor or edit an untrusted model's work. Trusted doesn't mean perfect or always truthful; it means not expected to intentionally subvert the protocol.

terms.short: Using a trusted model to review an untrusted model's actions and flag suspicious ones for review.
terms.definition: The worker proposes an action, the monitor scores how concerning it looks, and high-risk cases are blocked or sent to a human before running. The monitor is assumed not to help the attacker, but being weaker it may miss subtle problems. Human review budgets and thresholds set the tradeoff between safety and usefulness.

terms.short: An improved logit lens that learns a small translator for each layer before reading predictions.
terms.definition: Where the logit lens reads every draft with the final editor's eyes, the tuned lens trains a simple per-layer adapter to translate each draft first. This gives more faithful views of intermediate predictions. It is still a readout tool and doesn't by itself show causal mechanisms.

terms.short: Scanning a sequence with two positions that move toward each other or in step.
terms.definition: To check a palindrome, compare the first and last letters, then move both inward. It often turns an O(n²) brute force into O(n). It works best on sorted arrays or symmetric problems.

terms.short: The final step that turns a model's internal vector into a score for every token in the vocabulary.
terms.definition: It is the reverse of the embedding: from meaning-space back to word choices. The resulting scores are the logits, which softmax turns into probabilities. The logit lens applies it to middle layers.

terms.short: Written reasoning that leaves out, distorts or invents what actually drove the model's answer.
terms.definition: Someone gives a neat explanation for a decision but leaves out the hint that really influenced them. Experiments plant hints that change a model's answer and check whether its reasoning mentions them; often it does not. This limits how much a chain of thought can be trusted as a record of the computation.

terms.short: A structure that tracks which items belong to the same group and merges groups quickly.
terms.definition: Like tracking which islands are connected by bridges as new bridges are built. With path compression and union by rank, operations are nearly O(1). It is used for connected components and cycle detection.

terms.short: Trying to remove specific knowledge, data influence or behavior from an already trained model.
terms.definition: It is like trying to erase one lesson from a notebook that has no separate page for it, because a model's knowledge is spread across many weights. Methods update or retrain weights to suppress the target. Suppressed knowledge can sometimes be recovered with a little extra training, so 'unlearned' rarely means truly gone.

terms.short: In AI control, a model that might try to subvert the safety setup, so it is checked.
terms.definition: It is treated like a talented new contractor whose work is checked before it reaches production. Usually it is the most capable model, which is why it is useful and why it is hard to verify. Untrusted doesn't mean known to be malicious; it means safety must hold even if it is.

terms.short: Using a capable but untrusted model as a monitor, with checks in case it colludes.
terms.definition: A strong monitor can catch subtle problems a weaker one would miss, but it might also deliberately overlook them or coordinate with the worker. Protocols counter this by testing the monitor on planted attacks and limiting shared signals. Simply asking the monitor to be honest does not remove the risk.

terms.short: How much extra ability an AI gives someone compared with what they could do without it.
terms.definition: Two groups solve the same puzzle, one with a helper and one without; uplift is the difference. Studies compare people with AI access against a fair baseline, such as ordinary internet access, measuring success, speed or quality. It is the key quantity for judging misuse risk.

terms.short: Data held back from training and used to tune settings and choose between models.
terms.definition: It's the practice exam you check yourself against while studying. You can look at it many times, which means it slowly stops being a fair test. That is why a separate untouched test set is kept for the final score.

terms.short: A database that finds stored items whose embeddings are most similar to a query's embedding.
terms.definition: Instead of matching exact words, it finds passages that mean similar things, like a librarian who understands your question. It is the usual search engine behind RAG. Similarity search can still miss relevant but differently phrased content.

terms.short: The fixed set of tokens a model can read and produce.
terms.definition: Typical vocabularies have tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand tokens. Every next-token prediction is a choice over the whole vocabulary. Words outside it are spelled out from smaller pieces.

terms.short: Testing whether a strong model trained with a weaker supervisor's labels can outperform that supervisor.
terms.definition: A student may have skills a weaker teacher can't fully demonstrate. Researchers use a weaker model's labels to train a stronger pretrained model and see how much of the strong model's ability comes through. It is an analogy for humans supervising AI smarter than them.

terms.short: Protecting a model's weights from theft or unauthorized copying.
terms.definition: Like guarding the master blueprints for a powerful machine, it involves access controls, monitoring and secure infrastructure. Stolen weights let someone run or modify the model outside the developer's safeguards. Weights differ from chat transcripts or system prompts: they are the model itself.

terms.short: The learned numbers inside a model that determine how it turns inputs into outputs.
terms.definition: Think of them as millions or billions of tiny knobs that training adjusts. Model size is often given in parameters, like '8B' for eight billion. The weights are the model: copying them copies its capabilities.

terms.short: Studying a model with access to its internals: weights, activations and gradients.
terms.definition: It is like inspecting an engine with the hood open. White-box tools include probes, steering and circuit analysis, and they can catch things outputs don't reveal. They require access many outside evaluators don't have.
